title: List my URLs
idea: `GET /codes` returns only the URLs that belong to the logged-in user. The user comes from the verified token, never from the request.
points: `requireAuth` runs first and sets `req.user` from the verified token.
`where(eq(urls.userId, userId))` keeps other users' rows out of the result.
Without `orderBy`, Postgres promises no row order. `desc(urls.id)` lists newest first.
No rows is not an error: reply `200` with an empty array.

code.title: GET /codes
code.caption: Service, controller and route are new. Four callers use the same route.

walk.text: Name the three columns the response needs. Nothing else leaves the server.
The filter: only rows whose `user_id` equals the caller's id.
`orderBy` makes the order certain: newest first.
The id comes from `req.user`, never from the URL or the body.
Guard the route with `requireAuth`. Register it before `/:shortCode`.
Lecture 12's middleware, condensed: verify the token, then set `req.user`.
No token gives `401`. Each user sees only their own list. Alan has none: `200` with `[]`.

pitfalls: Never read the user id from the query string or body. Use `req.user.id`.
This route returns every row. Add `limit` and `offset` before lists get long.

quiz.q: Grace sends `GET /codes?userId=1` with her own token. What prints?
quiz.why: The service filters by `req.user.id`, the id inside the verified token. The query string is never read, so Grace sees only her one URL.

takeaway: Filter by the id from the verified token, never by a client-supplied id.
